text: The applicant was born in 1933.

The applicant submitted that since the 1974 Turkish intervention she had been deprived of her property rights, since her property was located in the area under the occupation and control of the Turkish military authorities.
The applicant made an attempt to return to her home and property on 19 July 1989 but was not allowed to do so by the Turkish military authorities.
The Turkish military authorities prevented the applicant from having access to and using her house and properties.
On 19 July 1989, the applicant joined an anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia.
The applicants in the Chrysostomos and Papachrysostomou v. Turkey case also took part in the anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia on 19 July 1989.
The applicant in the Loizidou v. Turkey case also took part in the anti-Turkish demonstration in the Ayios Kassianos area in Nicosia on 19 July 1989.
According to an affidavit sworn by the applicant before the Nicosia District Court on 4 August 2000, the demonstration of 19 July 1989 was peaceful.

text: In his report of 7 December 1989 on the UN operations in Cyprus, the UN Secretary General stated that in the evening of 19 July 1989, some 1,000 Greek Cypriot demonstrators, mostly women, forced their way into the UN buffer zone in the Ayios Kassianos area of Nicosia.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the demonstrators broke through a wire barrier maintained by UNFICYP and destroyed an UNFICYP observation post.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the demonstrators broke through the line formed by UNFICYP soldiers and entered a former school complex where UNFICYP reinforcements regrouped to prevent them from proceeding further.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, a short while later Turkish-Cypriot police and security forces elements forced their way into the area and apprehended 111 persons, 101 of them women.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the Ayios Kassianos school complex is situated in the UN buffer zone, but the Turkish forces claim it to be on their side of the cease-fire line.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, under working arrangements with UNFICYP, the Turkish-Cypriot security forces had patrolled the Ayios Kassianos school grounds for several years within specific restrictions, and this patrolling had ceased altogether as part of the unmanning agreement implemented the previous May.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, in the afternoon of 21 July 1989, some 300 Greek Cypriots gathered at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia to protest the continuing detention by the Turkish-Cypriot authorities of those apprehended at Ayios Kassianos.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the number of demonstrators at the main entrance to the UN protected area in Nicosia fluctuated between 200 and 2,000 and they blocked all UN traffic through this entrance until 30 July 1989, when the Turkish-Cypriot authorities released the last two detainees.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the events of 19 July 1989 created considerable tension in the island and intensive efforts were made, both at the UN headquarters and at Nicosia, to contain and resolve the situation.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, on 21 July 1989 the UN Secretary General expressed his concern at the events that had taken place and stressed that it was vital that all parties keep in mind the purpose of the UN buffer zone as well as their responsibility to ensure that that area was not violated.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the UN Secretary General urged the Turkish-Cypriot authorities to release without delay all those who had been detained.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, on 24 July 1989 the President of the Security Council announced that he had conveyed to the representatives of all the parties, on behalf of the members of the Council, the Council's deep concern at the tense situation created by the incidents of 19 July 1989.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

text: According to the UN Secretary General's report of 7 December 1989, the President of the Security Council stressed the need strictly to respect the UN buffer zone and appealed for the immediate release of all persons still detained.
section_path: C. The UN Secretary General's report

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code defines an unlawful assembly as occurring where five or more persons assemble with intent to commit an offence, or, being assembled with intent to carry out some common purpose, conduct themselves in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear that the persons so assembled will commit a breach of the peace, or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to commit a breach of the peace.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that it is immaterial that the original assembly was lawful if, being assembled, the persons conduct themselves with a common purpose in such a manner as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear a breach of the peace.

Section 70 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that when an unlawful assembly has begun to execute the purpose for which it assembled by a breach of the peace and to the terror of the public, the assembly is called a riot and the persons assembled are said to be riotously assembled.
According to section 71 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, any person who takes part in an unlawful assembly is guilty of a misdemeanour and liable to imprisonment for one year.

Section 80 of the Cypriot Criminal Code provides that any person who carries in public without lawful occasion any offensive arm or weapon in such a manner as to cause terror to any person is guilty of a misdemeanour and is liable to imprisonment for two years, and his arms or weapons shall be forfeited.
According to section 82 of the Cypriot Criminal Code, it is an offence to carry a knife outside the home.
